_comment: English narration for Part 3, 'Through the smoke'. Same scene ids and
figures as narasiRadar.json; tts_konsesi.py --film radar --bahasa en.

teks.01-kilas: In Part 2, we found damaged peat inside four concessions on the Ketapang coast that burned wider and longer. This time we follow the fire through the season: when it arrived, and where it went.
teks.02-asap: But at the height of the fires, optical satellites could barely see the ground. On the second of September, smoke plumes stretched from the coast. Five days later, haze covered the whole area.
teks.03-jam: Heat-detecting satellites catch the fire's heat twice a day, even through thin smoke. From July to October, they recorded more than a hundred and twenty thousand detections on this coast. The fire spread from early August, and peaked at the end of that month.
teks.04-radar: To see the ground beneath the smoke, we need radar. Sentinel-1 radar uses a wavelength of five point six centimetres. Over peat and scrub, its signal loses coherence within twelve days. The new NISAR satellite uses twenty-four centimetres. That long wave reaches through the canopy, and its signal stays coherent.
teks.05-peta: Fire breaks that coherence, and changes the radar echo. From thirty-five image pairs on four orbit tracks, NISAR flagged about eighty thousand hectares as burned. Seven in ten match the burn mapped by Sentinel-2. These NISAR data are still provisional.
teks.06-pekan: Radar passes only every twelve days, so its dates are rough. But both clocks agree. Inside the four concessions, the fire arrived four to seven days earlier than on similar unpermitted land around them. Before September, eight in ten fire locations inside had already ignited. Outside, two-thirds.
teks.07-batas: Did fire cross the boundary from outside in, or the other way round? Twenty-five burn scars straddle a concession boundary. Eight burned first inside, four outside, and thirteen within the same window. Radar passes too rarely to decide. Where fires started is still read from the heat detections, as in Part 2.
teks.08-tutup: Radar sees through the smoke and confirms where the ground burned, but not yet on which day. The heat detections give the clock; radar gives the proof on the ground. Both show the same thing: inside the four concessions, fire came earlier, and the land just outside the boundary burned on the same days. Drier peat does catch fire sooner, but that is still a hypothesis to be tested.
